subject: pe
topicDisplay: Socio Cultural Issues In Physical Activity And Sport
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Hawk-Eye and goal-line technology are examples of technology used primarily to:
options: Aid officiating and improve decision accuracy
questions.explain: Such technologies support officials by providing accurate evidence for decisions, improving fairness.

questions.q: Historically, sport was more accessible to the upper classes largely because they had:
options: Time, money and access to facilities
questions.explain: The upper classes had the leisure time, money and facilities to participate, unlike many workers.

questions.q: 'Broken-time payments' in early sport referred to:
options: Compensation to working men for lost wages while playing
questions.explain: Broken-time payments compensated working-class players for wages lost while playing, a step towards professionalism.

questions.q: The boycotts of the 1980 Moscow and 1984 Los Angeles Olympics best illustrate sport being used for:
questions.explain: The Cold War boycotts show how governments use sport as a political tool to make statements.

questions.q: Rational recreation in the industrial era is best described as sport that was:
questions.explain: Rational recreation involved regular, regulated and codified sports developed in the urban industrial era.

questions.q: The Olympic ideal as expressed by de Coubertin emphasised that the most important thing is:
options: Taking part and the struggle, not the triumph
questions.explain: The Olympic ideal stresses participation, fair play and the struggle rather than winning alone.

questions.q: The 'win-at-all-costs' (Lombardian) ethic is best contrasted with:
options: Both the counter-culture and amateur fair-play ethics
questions.explain: The win-at-all-costs Lombardian ethic contrasts with the counter-culture and fair-play participation ethics.

questions.q: Commercialisation of sport is best defined as:
options: Treating sport as a commodity to generate profit
questions.explain: Commercialisation treats sport as a business or commodity managed primarily to make money.

questions.q: An amateur in the Victorian sense was a performer who:
options: Always came from the working class
Was paid a salary to compete
Competed for the love of the game, not money
questions.explain: Amateurs played for enjoyment and the love of sport rather than for financial reward.

questions.q: Pre-industrial 'mob football' is best characterised as:
options: Local, occasional, violent and with few rules
questions.explain: Pre-industrial mob games were local, infrequent, violent and had simple, unwritten, varying rules.

questions.q: The 19th-century concept of a well-rounded sporting gentleman combining sport and morality is called:
options: The cult of athleticism / muscular Christianity
questions.explain: Athleticism (muscular Christianity) combined physical endeavour with moral integrity and character building.

questions.q: A 'glass ceiling' as a barrier to participation refers to:
options: An invisible barrier limiting progress, e.g. women into leadership roles
questions.explain: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier preventing under-represented groups from reaching higher positions.

questions.q: Which best describes 'shamateurism' in sport's history?
options: Athletes who were amateurs in name but paid covertly
A type of fair play award
questions.explain: Shamateurism describes nominally amateur athletes who received hidden or under-the-table payments.

questions.q: Spectator violence at football, including organised fighting between fans, is referred to as:
questions.explain: Hooliganism is disorderly, often violent behaviour by spectators associated particularly with football.

questions.q: The Paralympic Games most directly help to address barriers relating to:
questions.explain: The Paralympics raise the profile of disability sport and challenge barriers for disabled performers.

questions.q: Stereotyping that certain sports are 'unfeminine' is a barrier to participation relating to:
questions.explain: Gender stereotyping and myths about appropriateness can discourage female participation in some sports.

questions.q: Which is given as a reason why some athletes choose to take performance-enhancing drugs?
options: The pressure to win and associated rewards and fame
questions.explain: Pressure to win, financial rewards, fame and the belief others are doping can drive PED use.

questions.q: Which is a potential negative effect of commercialisation on sport?
options: More media coverage of minority sports
Rule changes and scheduling to suit sponsors and TV
questions.explain: Commercial pressures can alter rules, timings and breaks to suit broadcasters and sponsors rather than players.

questions.q: The use of technology giving some athletes an advantage based on cost raises concerns about:
questions.explain: Expensive equipment can create unfair advantages and inequality, sometimes called technological doping.

questions.q: Globalisation of sport is best illustrated by:
options: Worldwide broadcasting and migration of athletes between nations
questions.explain: Globalisation involves the worldwide spread of sport through media, migration of athletes and global markets.

questions.q: Which factor of post-1850 urban-industrial Britain most encouraged the spread of rational sport?
options: Improved transport, more free time and codification
questions.explain: Better transport, the Saturday half-day and codified rules allowed regular, organised competition.

questions.q: Positive deviance in sport, such as overtraining through injury, is best described as:
options: Over-conformity to the norms and values of sport
questions.explain: Positive deviance is excessive over-conformity to sporting values, such as playing through serious injury.

questions.q: A strategy used by anti-doping bodies such as WADA to deter drug use is:
options: Out-of-competition testing and the athlete whereabouts system
questions.explain: WADA uses random out-of-competition testing and whereabouts requirements to detect and deter doping.

questions.q: A classification used to ensure fair competition in disability sport groups athletes by:
questions.explain: Classification systems group athletes by impairment and functional ability to ensure fair competition.

questions.q: A criticism of increased use of technology in officiating is that it can:
options: Disrupt the flow and momentum of the game
questions.explain: Reviewing decisions with technology can interrupt the flow, delay play and reduce spectator atmosphere.

questions.q: Deviance in sport is best defined as behaviour that:
options: Goes against the moral values and norms of society or sport
questions.explain: Deviance is behaviour that breaks the accepted norms, values and rules of sport or wider society.

questions.q: Underrepresentation of some ethnic groups in coaching despite playing success is sometimes explained by:
questions.explain: Stacking and institutional discrimination can limit ethnic minorities' access to leadership and coaching roles.

questions.q: The 19th-century English public schools are credited with:
options: Codifying and spreading games through athleticism
questions.explain: Public schools codified games and promoted athleticism, spreading organised sport via their pupils.

questions.q: A drawback for an athlete who is heavily reliant on sponsorship is that they may:
options: Lose income or face pressure if performance or behaviour disappoints sponsors
questions.explain: Sponsors may withdraw funding if an athlete underperforms or behaves badly, creating pressure and instability.

questions.q: Wearable performance trackers and GPS vests are an example of technology used mainly to:
options: Monitor and improve athlete training and performance
questions.explain: GPS and wearables provide data on workload and movement to optimise training and reduce injury.
